prize_parts.citation: for conceptual and empirical analyses showing how technological change and international trade reshape labour demand, wage inequality and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: one part, B009, crediting Autor, Katz and Hanson. The discussion sharpened my reasons for it but did not change the choice. The achievement is one explanatory account of how labour demand responds to technology and trade. Katz anchors the long-run evidence on the supply of and demand for skills and on the wage structure. Autor links the task and polarisation evidence to the trade strand. Hanson, with Autor and Dorn, supplies the quasi-experimental evidence that trade-induced adjustment costs are large, local and persistent. The skill-premium evidence is the older and better-confirmed half, and the trade-shock evidence is the sharper-designed half. Each strand needs the other for the result to be read as more than one empirical episode. Both have been replicated, contested and refined for more than a decade, with foundational work from the early 1990s, so maturity is not in doubt. On the chair's question about the 2023 and 2024 prizes, the round-1 exchange describes them as recognising women's labour-market outcomes (Goldin) and how institutions shape prosperity (Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson). On that description, the overlap with B009 is thematic. Neither citation recognised the empirical wage-structure and trade-adjustment evidence, and a citation confined to that evidence leaves task theory to others. I would write it as a concrete test of the citation, not a slogan: the wording above says 'conceptual and empirical analyses' and claims no theory of automation or directed technology, so Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo are not credited by implication. I treat support counts as irrelevant to merit. The B009 split between two trios is an attribution question, not a doubt about scientific quality.
statement.case_against: Dorn is a full co-author of the China-shock papers, and the three-name cap forces his exclusion. That is a real cost, and it falls on the strand with the sharpest identification. The task framework rests partly on people who are not credited. The citation can only mitigate this by wording. A committee could reasonably see technology and trade as two achievements, in which case a single citation reads as two prizes in one and bundles unlike evidence. The persistence, magnitude and external validity of the China-shock estimates, and the inference properties of shift-share designs, remain debated. Katz also appears in B050, though I see no real double counting. Finally, my own earlier work on capital-skill complementarity is in the same literature, which could make me too receptive to the skill-premium strand. I discount my Katz preference for that reason and still find that the broader citation is the more defensible.

responses.point: Teorell proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn, centred on the credible and replicated China-shock evidence. He says that if the committee defines the discovery as the broader technology, tasks and trade picture, Katz belongs in it and Dorn is the likelier omission, but that the committee should say plainly that the China-shock co-author is being left out.
responses.response: The chair asked whether I would take the Dorn trio under the narrower definition. I would: Autor, Dorn and Hanson is a coherent and exact attribution of the trade-shock design, and I would vote for it over a split result. I still prefer Katz, because that narrower citation rests on the part of the evidence with the most open questions about persistence and inference, and it drops the long-run wage-structure evidence that gives the shock its interpretation. I accept your demand for transparency. If the Katz trio is adopted, the committee record should state that the cap, not a judgement about contribution, excludes Dorn.

responses.point: Andersson answers my opening question on B045. He argues that a methods contribution should not rank below a discovery by default, because BLP changed what can be measured, and he cites merger review and thirty years of scrutiny. He also concedes that Bresnahan and the dynamic-industry work complicate attribution.
responses.response: I accept your correction. My question was about breadth, and I did not mean that methods rank below discoveries. BLP has an unusually clean record of use in practice and a clean three-name core. That moves B045 up in my own estimate, though not above my alternatives. Two things hold me back. The citation has to choose between demand estimation and the dynamic-industry line, and the credited names leave out Bresnahan. Your own list of uncertainties says as much. Compared with B009, the evidence of changed understanding is narrower in reach. I would not oppose a B045 prize on method grounds, and I do not put B045 in my alternatives only because I still compare it with B014 as a single compact discovery.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B014 for its compact and better-bounded core of Melitz and Helpman, and argues that B009 bundles skill-biased change, tasks and trade shocks. He also says a B009 prize needs Autor, Hanson and Katz, so Dorn's omission is a real cost.
responses.response: Your last sentence is the closest to my own view of the Katz trio. I do not dispute that B014 is the more compact discovery, and that is why it is my first alternative. The chair asked what would move me to B014. It would be a committee judgement that technology and trade cannot be written as one citation without becoming a composite, or that the Dorn-or-Katz choice cannot be settled. Then a single clean pair would be preferable to a contested trio. I do not think we are there. The strands share one object, labour-market adjustment to changing demand, and your citation is just as bounded once the uncredited priority claims of Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum are taken seriously. I also cannot use field balance after Krugman 2008 to weigh against merit.

responses.point: Hassler, as chair, moved from B040 to B009 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. He would write the citation around labour-demand evidence on technology and trade rather than a theory of automation, and he regards a Dorn variant as defensible if the committee prefers the trade-shock framing.
responses.response: I agree with the wording discipline, and my citation follows it by naming conceptual and empirical analyses and not a theory of technology. I also share your acceptance that Dorn in place of Katz is a defensible variant. One difference: you describe the technology and trade strands as converging, and I would add that their evidential statuses differ. The skill-premium evidence is long confirmed, and the China-shock magnitudes are still debated. That is an argument for keeping both strands in the citation, not for choosing between them. On B040, I take your point that its attribution is cleaner than B009's. I still weigh specification sensitivity in the cross-country evidence and the closer thematic proximity to the 2024 prize more heavily than you now do.

uncertainties: Whether the committee defines the achievement as the broader technology, tasks and trade account of labour demand, which favours Katz, or as the China-shock and local adjustment evidence, which favours Dorn. I cannot resolve this from the evidence provided.
How persistent and how large the China-shock effects are, and how far they generalise beyond the United States, given the shift-share inference debate.
Whether a citation worded around empirical and conceptual analysis can credit the task framework fairly without implying priority over Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo.
Whether the committee reads the 2023 and 2024 citations as leaving B009 untouched. Members have described those prizes in somewhat different terms.
Whether B014 overtakes B009 if the Dorn-or-Katz choice and the bundling issue cannot be settled, given that B014's own uncredited priority claims and welfare-gain critique remain.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from round 1. No recusal-level connection to Autor, Katz or Hanson is apparent from the supplied profile. Profile-based connections: I have co-authored with Timo Boppart and have long-standing co-authors including John Hassler, the chair. My capital-skill complementarity work (with Ohanian, Ríos-Rull and Violante) is in the same literature on technology and wage inequality as B009, and I flag that this familiarity could incline me toward the skill-premium strand and Katz. None of those co-authors is a proposed laureate. My own work is also cited in the 2018 Scientific Background for other topics, and none of that bears on any shortlisted candidate. These are disclosed and not adjudicated, and I claim no independent verification.
